reference.title: The story of the ice cream sellers
reference.text: Have you ever noticed that you often find the same kinds of shops together in the same street? Economics gives us one explanation. When two ice cream sellers share a beach, the best situation for the customers is when each seller is in the middle of their half. But each seller wants more customers, so they both move to the middle and end up next to each other. So what’s good for businesses isn’t always good for customers.

exercises.situation: You are a classmate in an English class (level: pre-intermediate). You look at photos of eight global chain stores: Zara, Apple, Topshop, The Body Shop, H&M, Nike, IKEA and Uniqlo. Ask the student, one at a time: What do they sell? Do you know which country they started in? (Zara – Spain, Apple and Nike – the USA, Topshop and The Body Shop – the UK, H&M and IKEA – Sweden, Uniqlo – Japan.) Do you have them in your country or city? If not, would you like to have them? Why (not)? Do you ever buy from their websites? What other big chain stores are there in your city? Which chain stores do you go to most often? Do you prefer shopping at chain stores or independent shops? Why? Give short answers about yourself too. If the student makes a mistake with present simple questions or shopping words, repeat the correct form naturally.

exercises.opener: Look at these shops! Do you know what they all sell?

tasks.context: The story of the ice cream sellers. Imagine a beach a kilometre long, full of sunbathers. The sun is shining, the sea is warm. An ice cream seller called George arrives. Where does he put his ice cream cart? Obviously, (1) …, where the sunbathers can easily walk to him and buy an ice cream. Later that day, a second ice cream seller, Georgina, arrives. George and Georgina talk for a while and decide that the best solution is this: (2) …, and they each put their ice cream cart in the middle of their half. In zone A of the beach the customers go to George, and in zone B they go to Georgina. This is good for the customers, because nobody needs to walk more than 250 metres for an ice cream. But George isn’t happy – he only has 50% of the customers that he had before. So (3) … . Zone A is now bigger than zone B, and George has more customers and makes more money, but some of his customers need to walk 500 metres to get their ice cream. Of course, Georgina sees what George has done, and now she isn’t happy – she’s going to lose money. So (4) …, and gets 50% of the customers again. The result is this: George and Georgina end up next to each other. They both get 50% of the customers. More customers need to walk further for an ice cream. So what’s good for businesses isn’t always good for customers.

reference.title: Present perfect for experiences
reference.text: We use the present perfect to talk about past experiences in your life, when we don’t say when they happened: She’s been to New York three times. Have you ever been to Ikea? I’ve never met Nina’s husband. He’s seen that film twice. ever = at any time in your life (in questions); never = at no time (with a + verb).

reference.title: Present perfect or past simple?
reference.text: Conversations often begin in the present perfect (a general question about experience) and then change to the past simple (details: when, where, what): Have you ever been to Mexico? Yes, I have. When did you go there? I went last year. Jack’s broken his leg. Oh no! When did that happen? Yesterday. He broke it playing football. With a finished time (yesterday, last year, three weeks ago) use the past simple.

reference.title: been or gone?
rows: He went to Paris and came back.

reference.wrong: I’ve been to H&M three weeks ago.
reference.right: I went to H&M three weeks ago.
reference.why: An exact past time (three weeks ago) needs the past simple.

tasks.instruction: Answer the questions in d about you
tasks.note: WB 3e — о себе → Write

exercises.prompt: Answer the questions about you. If you have done something, write a sentence about the last time you did it.

questions.text: Have you ever bought something on eBay?
questions.hint: (Yes, I have. I bought… / No, I haven’t.)

questions.text: Have you ever booked a flight online?
Have you ever stayed in an Airbnb house or flat?
questions.hint: (Yes, I have. I stayed… / No, I’ve never…)

criteria: short answers Yes, I have / No, I haven’t
details about the last time in the past simple (I bought…, I booked…, I stayed…)
no present perfect with a finished time (not I’ve booked it last year)

tasks.instruction: Complete with the present perfect or the past simple of the verb in brackets. Use contractions.

exercises.text: {} you ever {} to Japan?
Yes, I have. I {} there in 2019.
I {} this jacket in the sales last week.
She {} never {} anything online.
exercises.explain: never + present perfect: She’s never sold…

exercises.text: When {} you {} your new phone?
exercises.explain: When…? asks about a finished time → past simple.

exercises.text: We {} that film twice. It’s brilliant.
exercises.explain: Experience, how many times → present perfect.

exercises.text: Tom {} his leg. He {} it playing football yesterday.
exercises.explain: News → present perfect; the detail (yesterday) → past simple.

exercises.text: I {} a lot of money when I was on holiday in Rome.
exercises.explain: A finished time (when I was on holiday) → past simple.

tasks.instruction: Write questions with Have you ever…? Then write the past simple question in brackets.

exercises.prompt: you / lose / your keys / ?
answers: Have you ever lost your keys?

exercises.prompt: Where / you / lose / them?
answers: Where did you lose them?

exercises.prompt: you / buy / clothes online / ?
answers: Have you ever bought clothes online?

exercises.prompt: What / you / buy?
answers: What did you buy?

exercises.prompt: your parents / fly / to America / ?
answers: Have your parents ever flown to America?

exercises.prompt: your brother / meet / a famous person / ?
answers: Has your brother ever met a famous person?

tasks.instruction: Correct the mistake in each sentence. Write the sentence.

exercises.prompt: I’ve bought these shoes last Saturday.
answers: I bought these shoes last Saturday.

exercises.prompt: Did you ever sell anything on eBay?
answers: Have you ever sold anything on eBay?
exercises.explain: Life experience with ever → present perfect.

exercises.prompt: When have you arrived?
answers: When did you arrive?

exercises.prompt: Sarah isn’t here. She’s been to the shops.
answers: Sarah isn’t here. She’s gone to the shops.
Sarah isn’t here. She has gone to the shops.

exercises.prompt: He has never went to IKEA.
answers: He has never been to IKEA.
He’s never been to IKEA.
exercises.explain: Experience of a place → been; went is past simple.

exercises.prompt: I have saw that film twice.
answers: I have seen that film twice.
I’ve seen that film twice.
